notes: Edition composed by Claude from the collected headlines, reading titles and metadata only.
Each narrative is an idea that joins several different events; what it joins is listed at the top. It commits to a claim, and the last rung of every narrative is the case against it. Read both.
Where a narrative continues one from the previous edition it says what has changed since; every edition is kept, so the reader can step back to where we were.

A narrative may also resume one that stopped in the last four weeks ('resumes' gives that edition's stamp and the narrative's id), and may be written from a subject the site's notebook has been keeping ('builds'); such a narrative can cite headlines from earlier days, each shown with its date, beside at least three of the day's own.

Each narrative ends with 'How we got here': four horizons, since 2020, since 2008, since 1989 and since 1945, each the start of a regime the headlines are living inside, and sometimes a fifth that reaches further back and names its own starting year. They are a trajectory, not a verdict.

Each narrative sets one or two things to watch for: what should follow, by when, if its join is right. Later editions check them against their headlines; the ledger is data/watch.json and the count stands beside the narrative's firmness.

Each narrative looks ahead: the precedent its join most resembles, two or three paths with one favoured, and where the trajectory points over a decade. That is the writer's anticipation, drawn on what it knows of history and not only on the headlines; the expectations are the earliest dated signs of the favoured path, and are how the site checks it.
The connections are made by the model, not by the publishers. Follow any headline to the original report before repeating it.
Books and trajectories appear only where they change how a fragment or a horizon reads.

readings.line: The chip scandal has not cut the chipmaker's sales, and the burden of proof now falls on the countries its chips pass through.

watch.what: A Southeast Asian government or business group says the US chip proposal would cost it data-centre investment or projects.
watch.because: If the cost of the scandal is being moved onto transit states rather than the seller, those states will be the first to count and protest it.

watch.what: Reports of Huang's 1 December hearing say lawmakers pressed Nvidia on sales routed through Singapore, Malaysia or other Southeast Asian hubs.
watch.because: The join holds that the scandal is now about the places chips pass through, so the hearing should turn on routes and hubs rather than on one man's conduct.

ahead.precedent: The closest case is COCOM, the western embargo committee of 1949 to 1994. When Toshiba Machine and Norway's Kongsberg sold propeller-milling machines to Moscow in 1987, the Japanese and Norwegian firms were punished and their governments tightened their checks, while American suppliers kept selling. A nearer case is Nvidia's A800 and H800 chips, built to fit the October 2022 rules: Washington widened the rules in October 2023 and the company's revenue kept rising. The present differs because the countries now asked to police are the ones hosting the data centres.

paths.name: Transit states adopt US-style permits
paths.text: By early 2027 Singapore and Malaysia publish permit and end-user checks for advanced AI chips to keep their trusted status, and Nvidia's sales continue to grow. The Fortune report of Singapore defending itself and the Megaspeed inquiry show the pressure is already on the hubs, and they have more to lose from exclusion than from compliance.
paths.sign: Singapore or Malaysia announces a permit requirement for exports or re-exports of high-end AI chips.

paths.name: Allies push back, rule narrowed
paths.text: Objections from allies, which Handelsblatt already reports, and from Singapore lead Commerce to exempt trusted hubs or delay the Southeast Asia rule after the 1 December hearing. This is less likely because the administration needs to show action after the scandal.
paths.sign: The Commerce Department delays or narrows its Southeast Asia chip proposal after allied objections.

paths.name: Seller made liable
paths.text: Congress makes chipmakers legally responsible for re-exports by their customers, and Nvidia's sales slow. Nothing in the headlines points this way: the board's own committee is the kind of measure that usually heads off such a law.
paths.sign: A bill is introduced making chip sellers liable for re-export of their products by third parties.

ahead.decade: Over ten years export control moves from a list kept in Washington to a licensing system run by every country that hosts large computing, with the chipmakers' sales protected and the policing done by the importers.

readings.change: Since 13 November the US has proposed extending AI chip controls to Southeast Asia, Singapore has defended its standing and a Singaporean firm, Megaspeed, is under US investigation. Nvidia reported revenue up 103% and a $150bn buyback, its board refused Jensen Huang's return and set up an export-control committee, and Huang will testify to Congress on 1 December.
readings.claim: On the day Nvidia reported revenue up 103% and a further $150bn buyback, Fortune reported Singapore defending its status after Washington proposed AI chip controls for Southeast Asia, LB.ua reported a US inquiry into Singapore's Megaspeed, Handelsblatt reported allies unsettled by Trump's new chip rules, and a Chinese envoy attacked Dutch curbs on ASML. Nvidia's board refused Huang's return and formed its own export-control committee, and Huang will appear before the House on 1 December. The scandal over chips reaching China is being settled by placing new duties on the states and firms the chips travel through, while the company that sold them reports its best quarter.

fragments.label: Results and buyback
fragments.text: China's 163.com reported Nvidia's third-quarter revenue up 103% with guidance above expectations, and a board approval for a further $150bn share buyback. Taiwan's United Daily News put revenue at $115.8bn with next-quarter guidance of up to $130bn, and said the forecast lifted the shares 4% after hours while the semiconductor index stopped falling. Jornal de Brasília and DW's Spanish service reported the same doubling.

fragments.label: The board and the former chief
fragments.text: 163.com said the board explicitly rejected Jensen Huang's return, after Anadolu in Turkey and El Mundo in Spain quoted him saying he would be honoured to lead the company again if asked. Malaysia's The Star reported that the board had formed a committee for national security and export control oversight. UDN said the US House confirmed Huang will attend a hearing on 1 December, and Argentina's El Litoral and Vietnam's Dân trí reported the summons.

fragments.label: Singapore and Southeast Asia
fragments.text: Fortune reported that Singapore defended its status as a 'trusted business hub' after the US proposed extending AI chip controls to Southeast Asia. Ukraine's LB.ua reported a US investigation into the Singaporean company Megaspeed over chips for China. Germany's Handelsblatt headlined that, in the Nvidia affair, Trump's new chip rules unsettle allies.

fragments.label: The Netherlands and China
fragments.text: International Business Times UK quoted a Chinese envoy saying Dutch export curbs on ASML reflect Europe's fear that China will 'rob' its technology. The complaint is addressed to The Hague, which issues the licences, not to Washington, which wanted the curbs.

fragments.label: Duties move outward
fragments.text: The headlines put the work of stopping chips reaching China on Singapore's reputation, on a Singaporean firm under investigation and on Dutch licensing, while the American seller answers through a board committee and a hearing. Nothing in the quarter reported shows any loss of sales. The scandal began as a question about one executive and is being settled as obligations on the places chips pass through.

fragments.label: Investors read sales, not scandal
fragments.text: Sina Finance carried a Bank of America survey showing fund managers cut tech holdings by the largest margin in 20 years, and The Star wrote of a shaky semiconductor trade looking for a bottom. Those doubts are about the price of the AI boom. Nvidia's shares still rose after hours on its results, which suggests investors treat the scandal as a matter for regulators and transit states rather than for the company's revenue.

fragments.label: Old policy under a new name
fragments.text: Chip diversion through Singapore and Malaysia was a known problem before this scandal, and Dutch limits on ASML sales to China date from 2023, so the rules may simply continue existing policy that the scandal now gives a name to. Nvidia's quarter reflects orders placed months ago and cannot show whether the scandal will cost it sales later. The board's refusal of Huang and the 1 December hearing are real costs the company does bear.

fragments.label: Where the events part
fragments.text: The events do not share an actor or a motive. One is a company's earnings, one a proposed American rule, one a Dutch licensing decision attacked by a Chinese diplomat, and one an inquiry into a private firm. Only Handelsblatt ties the new rules to the affair in its headline; the rest could have been reported in a month with no scandal at all.

horizons.label: Since 2020
horizons.text: In October 2022 the US Commerce Department barred sales of the most advanced AI chips and chipmaking tools to China, a month before ChatGPT turned those chips into the scarcest input of the decade. Nvidia answered with reduced versions, the A800 and H800, and Washington widened the rules in October 2023. In January 2025 the outgoing Biden administration published a diffusion rule sorting the world into tiers of trusted and untrusted buyers; the Trump administration withdrew it that May and promised something simpler. Meanwhile Singapore and Malaysia's Johor became hosts of large data centres, and in early 2025 Singapore charged men in a fraud case over servers suspected of holding Nvidia chips. The proposal Fortune reports, controls for Southeast Asia, returns to the tier idea by another route. This decade made one company's chips both the boom's main product and the main object of security law, so its revenue and the state's controls have grown together, as the 103% rise in these headlines shows.

horizons.label: Since 2008
horizons.text: After 2008 chipmaking concentrated in a few places: TSMC in Taiwan made the most advanced chips, ASML in the Netherlands the only machines for the finest layers, and Nvidia in California designed the chips that used them. China, the second economy by 2010, set out in its Made in China 2025 plan of 2015 to make its own. Washington used the concentration as a lever: a denial order against ZTE in 2018, Huawei's listing in May 2019, and pressure on The Hague, which withheld licences for ASML's most advanced machines from 2019 and widened its curbs in 2023. That is the background to the Chinese envoy's complaint to the Netherlands in International Business Times. The method was always to have allies and suppliers do the stopping, because American firms sold the chips and allies made the tools. The proposal for Southeast Asia extends the same method to the places where the chips are installed and run.

horizons.label: Since 1989
horizons.text: The end of the Cold War dissolved COCOM in 1994, and the Wassenaar Arrangement that followed in 1996 left export control to each member's own lists and judgement. The World Trade Organisation, from 1995, and China's entry in 2001 rested on the belief that goods should move and that the exporting state need not ask where they ended up. Singapore built its economy as an entrepôt on that belief: a port, a financial centre and a place where goods are re-exported with few questions asked. Its insistence in Fortune that it is a 'trusted business hub' appeals to that thirty-year order. The Megaspeed inquiry reported by LB.ua tests the other side of it: a hub earned trust by moving goods quickly, and is now asked to check where they go. The years since 1989 made transit a business, and the present dispute turns it into a duty with legal risk attached.

horizons.label: Since 1945
horizons.text: Computing began as a state project: wartime codebreaking, then the Dartmouth workshop of 1956 that named artificial intelligence with foundation money in a decade when governments paid for most research that mattered. Its export was controlled from the start. COCOM, set up in 1949, let Washington and its allies list what could not be sold to the Soviet bloc, and when Toshiba Machine and Norway's Kongsberg sold milling machines for submarine propellers to Moscow in 1987, it was the Japanese and Norwegian firms that were punished and their governments that had to tighten their checks. The pattern of the American state writing the rule and the allied state doing the policing is older than any firm in these headlines. What differs is that the controlled product is now built by a private company whose quarterly revenue, $115.8bn by UDN's report, exceeds the yearly output of many states.

readings.line: Before leaders meet over two wars, each side strikes bridges and islands, the crossings a settlement would have to assign.

watch.what: Reports from the Shenzhen meeting say Crimea, the Kerch crossing or shipping through the Strait of Hormuz was discussed by the leaders.
watch.because: If the bridges and islands are struck as bargaining positions, they should appear on the agenda the strikes were meant to shape.

watch.what: Russia or Ukraine proposes a mutual halt to strikes on bridges or energy sites as part of the talks.
watch.because: Targets chosen for their value at the table are the ones each side will offer to stop hitting in exchange for something.

ahead.precedent: Linebacker II, the American bombing of Hanoi and Haiphong from 18 to 29 December 1972, was ordered to push North Vietnam back to the Paris talks, and the accords signed on 27 January 1973 were close to the terms already drafted. In Korea from 1951 to 1953 both sides fought for hills during the armistice talks because their position fixed the final line. The present differs because one meeting bears on two wars at once, and its host, China, is a party to neither.

paths.name: Talks get dates, strikes continue
paths.text: The Shenzhen meeting produces a timetable for further talks but no halt, and strikes on bridges, power and Gulf bases continue through December as each side improves its position. The Finnish call for a clear timetable and Business Day's account of both Washington and Tehran playing for time point to process rather than settlement.
paths.sign: The leaders announce a date or venue for further talks with no pause in strikes.

paths.name: A partial halt on infrastructure
paths.text: Moscow and Kyiv agree a limited pause on strikes against energy or bridges, as Washington brokered briefly in March 2025. It is less likely to hold, because the crossings struck this week are worth more to each side as threats than as concessions.
paths.sign: Russia and Ukraine announce a halt to strikes on energy sites or bridges.

paths.name: Neighbours drawn into the fighting
paths.text: Strikes on Transcarpathia, Kuwait and Bahrain draw Hungary or a Gulf state into the wars directly. Each has so far answered with statements and rail restrictions, not force.
paths.sign: A NATO or Gulf state invokes collective defence after a strike on its territory.

ahead.decade: If ceasefire lines are again set by what each side holds when talks end, bridges, islands and straits become the places fought for in the last weeks of every war, and the people living beside them carry the longest risk.

readings.change: Since 13 November a meeting of Trump, Putin and Xi in Shenzhen has been fixed for 19 November. Ukraine has struck the Crimean Bridge two days running, Russia has hit two Kyiv bridges and left 700,000 households without power, and the US has struck Iran's Qeshm Island after Iranian attacks on Bahrain. The strikes have moved from bases and oil sites to crossings.
readings.claim: Ukraine struck the Crimean Bridge for a second day, Russia hit Kyiv's Yuzhny and Severny bridges and cut power and heating, a Russian strike on Transcarpathia led Hungary to restrict trains to Mukachevo, and the US struck Iran's Qeshm Island after Iranian attacks on Bahrain while Kuwait intercepted drones. All of it fell in the two days before Trump meets Putin and Xi in Shenzhen. The targets are links between territories: the only bridge to an annexed peninsula, bridges across the Dnipro, a rail line to an EU state, an island in the Strait of Hormuz and the island state that hosts a US fleet. Each side is striking what a settlement would have to assign, and the people who use those crossings pay first.

events.label: Ukraine hits Crimean Bridge again
Russia strikes Kyiv bridges and heating
Transcarpathia strike stops Hungarian trains
US strikes Qeshm after Bahrain attack
Drones over Kuwait, Gulf backs Bahrain
Three leaders set to meet

fragments.label: Crimea and Kyiv
fragments.text: Australia's Western Advocate reported Ukraine hitting Russia's bridge to Crimea for a second day, and UNIAN quoted a Ukrainian official saying 'we are only just beginning'. Kommersant reported Russia's defence ministry striking Kyiv's Yuzhny and Severny bridges; UNIAN said part of Kyiv lost heating and hot water, and Greece's ENIKOS counted 15 dead and 700,000 households without power. Lenta.RU reported Russia naming priority targets in reply to the Crimean Bridge attack.

fragments.label: A border rail line
fragments.text: UNIAN reported Hungary saying a Russian strike on Transcarpathia was 'hardly the last', and LB.ua that Hungary temporarily restricted rail service to Mukachevo. A link between an EU member and western Ukraine was cut by a strike, not by a decision in Budapest.

fragments.label: Qeshm and Bahrain
fragments.text: DW's Arabic and Spanish services reported US aircraft striking an Iranian missile base on Qeshm Island after a new Iranian attack on Bahrain. Xinhua quoted a US official calling the strikes 'self-defence', Anadolu quoted Iran saying several locations were hit, and Vietnam's Dân trí reported Tehran warning of retaliation.

fragments.label: Kuwait and the Gulf states
fragments.text: Egypt's Al-Youm Al-Sabea, Arab News and Israel's Walla reported Kuwait's army intercepting hostile drones. Lebanon's Al-Anbaa reported the Gulf Cooperation Council backing Bahrain's sovereignty, Al-Masry Al-Youm reported Egypt calling Gulf security part of its own, and Amman newspaper reported Jordan condemning continued Iranian attacks on Bahrain.

fragments.label: Crossings before a meeting
fragments.text: DIE WELT reported Witkoff and Kushner coming to Berlin and Trump meeting Putin and Xi on the same day, and Beijing's Jingbao wrote of the three heads of state about to appear together in Shenzhen. In the two days before, the targets in both wars were links rather than front positions: a bridge to Crimea, bridges across the Dnipro, a rail line to Hungary, an island in the Strait of Hormuz and Bahrain. These are what a settlement would have to assign or keep open, and striking them changes what each side can ask for.

fragments.label: A stalemate raises their value
fragments.text: South Africa's Business Day wrote that Trump and Tehran are gambling on time as the Iran war's stalemate deepens. When neither side expects to gain much ground, the power to close a crossing becomes the thing to trade. The cost of that position falls on Kyiv households without heat and on passengers between Hungary and Mukachevo.

fragments.label: The war's normal rhythm
fragments.text: The Crimean Bridge was struck in October 2022 and July 2023, and Russia has attacked Ukraine's power and heating every winter since 2022, so these strikes may be the war's usual November rather than moves timed to Shenzhen. The US called its Qeshm strike self-defence after an attack on Bahrain, a reply rather than a bid. No headline names the target of the Transcarpathia strike, which may not have been the rail line at all.

fragments.label: Where the events part
fragments.text: The events differ in who acts and on whom: a Ukrainian attack on a Russian military supply route, a Russian attack on a capital's civilian heating, an American reply to an attack on an ally, and drones over Kuwait whose sender no headline names. Only timing before one meeting joins them, and two wars that produce strikes every day will always produce some just before a summit.

horizons.label: Since 2020
horizons.text: Russia's invasion of February 2022 made infrastructure the main target of a European war. The Kerch bridge, opened in 2018, was damaged by a truck bomb in October 2022 and by sea drones in July 2023, and from October 2022 Russia struck Ukraine's power stations each winter. In March 2025 Washington brokered a short pause on energy strikes that each side accused the other of breaking. In June 2025 Ukrainian drones launched from lorries hit bombers deep inside Russia, and American bombers struck Fordow to end a twelve-day war between Israel and Iran. By these headlines the war with Iran has since closed the Strait of Hormuz and brought attacks on Gulf states. The decade's lesson in both wars is that cheap long-range drones let a side reach the other's crossings and power at any hour, so every round of talks now comes with strikes like those on the Kyiv bridges, chosen to show what can be reached.

horizons.label: Since 2008
horizons.text: Russia's war with Georgia in August 2008 and its annexation of Crimea in March 2014 made territory taken by force something Europe lived beside. The bridge to Crimea, built from 2015 to 2018, turned the annexation into a physical link, which is why Ukraine strikes it and why Lenta.RU reports Russia naming new targets in reply. In the Gulf, the nuclear agreement of July 2015 and Washington's withdrawal in May 2018 began a cycle of pressure and talks; in September 2019 drones and missiles halved Saudi output at Abqaiq for days without a declared war. Qeshm, beside Bandar Abbas, sits where Iran can threaten tankers in the strait. The years since 2008 produced both kinds of crossing struck this week: one built to hold an annexation, one held to threaten a shipping lane.

horizons.label: Since 1989
horizons.text: The Soviet collapse in 1991 left Crimea inside Ukraine and Transcarpathia on a new border with Hungary, the region whose rail link Hungary has now restricted. The Gulf War of 1991 brought American forces into the Gulf to stay; the Fifth Fleet was re-established in Bahrain in 1995, which is why an Iranian attack on Bahrain draws an American strike on Qeshm. The closest earlier use of bridges as bargaining came in 1999, when NATO aircraft destroyed the Danube bridges at Novi Sad during the Kosovo war to press Milošević to accept terms, which he did after 78 days. The invasion of Iraq in 2003 removed Iran's main regional enemy and made the Gulf the place where Iran and the United States face each other directly. Mary Kaldor's account of wars that blur front and rear describes the period's habit of fighting over the means of daily life rather than over lines on a map.

horizons.label: Since 1945
horizons.text: The rules these strikes are argued under were written after 1945. The Geneva Conventions of 1949 and the Additional Protocol of 1977, whose Article 54 forbids attacking what civilians need to survive and whose Article 56 protects dams and nuclear power stations, frame the dispute over Kyiv strikes that left 700,000 households without power. The meeting at the Great Bitter Lake in February 1945 began the American guarantee of the Gulf that the Qeshm strike enforces, and the Suez crisis of 1956 showed that a chokepoint is a political object and that the power underwriting it can change. Korea's armistice talks from 1951 to 1953, held while both armies fought for hills that fixed the final line, are the plainest case of fighting to shape a settlement. The present repeats that pattern, with bridges and islands rather than hills as the positions fought for.

readings.line: Two weeks of protest over prices and rents have been met with wage and pension top-ups, while the energy shock behind prices goes on.
readings.kicker: COST OF LIVING / THE STREET / COMPENSATION

watch.what: France's interior ministry reports a further national protest day with fewer than 146,000 taking part.
watch.because: If concessions compensate incomes without touching the cause, the protests should keep shrinking without stopping.

watch.what: Spain or Portugal announces a wage, benefit or tax relief measure, rather than a rent limit, in answer to the housing protests.
watch.because: The join holds that governments answer this wave by adding to incomes, not by acting on what sets rents and prices.

ahead.precedent: The gilets jaunes began on 17 November 2018, eight years before this collection. On 10 December 2018 Macron cancelled a fuel tax rise and announced 100 euros a month more for minimum-wage workers; the protests went on, smaller each Saturday, into spring 2019. The present differs because the wave runs in four countries at once, its Iberian half is about rents rather than fuel, and the price behind it comes from a war that no national tax can switch off.

paths.name: Top-ups, smaller protests to Christmas
paths.text: The 2027 budgets in Italy, France and Spain absorb further wage, pension and benefit increases, protest numbers keep falling through December, and the Porto and Lisbon housing camps stay as a smaller fixture. France's minimum wage acceleration and Italy's argument over 300 euros for pensioners show the answer governments have already chosen.
paths.sign: A European government announces a one-off payment or a higher indexation of wages or pensions for 2027.

paths.name: Rent limits in Spain or Portugal
paths.text: Spain or Portugal acts on rents with a national cap or a tax on tourist and empty flats, after the 11 November general strike. It is less likely in the coming weeks because both governments face landlords and tourism interests and budget fights that favour cash transfers.
paths.sign: Spain's or Portugal's cabinet approves a national rent limit or a new tax on tourist or empty flats.

paths.name: A shared European day of action
paths.text: Unions in several countries call a common strike date and the wave becomes a European movement. Nothing in the fortnight shows coordination across borders; each country's protest has its own calendar and grievance.
paths.sign: Unions in three or more European countries call a strike or protest on the same date.

ahead.decade: If energy shocks keep arriving through wars, European budgets will carry a standing line for compensating incomes, paid partly by tax brackets left unindexed, while housing remains the grievance that transfers do not reach.

readings.claim: Over two weeks, protest over living costs and housing has run in France, Spain, Portugal and Italy: 270,000 marched outside Paris on 6 November, Porto's housing camp put up tents on 8 November, Spain held its first general strike in 14 years on 11 November, Italy carried out searches in 13 cities on 14 November, and on 17 November France counted 146,000 at a new round. Governments have answered by adding to incomes, with France bringing forward a minimum wage rise on 10 November and Italy's coalition arguing this week over 300 euros for pensioners, while the European Commission says the energy shock is still raising prices and Brussels finds Spain collecting more than 2.5 billion euros from unindexed income tax brackets. The fortnight shows a wave that shrinks after each concession but does not stop, because the concessions compensate for prices without touching what sets them.

events.label: French protest rounds continue, smaller
Spain's general strike over housing
Portugal's housing encampments
Italy's searches and budget pension payment
Forecasts blame energy, taxes rise unseen
Minimum wage and benefits raised

fragments.label: France
fragments.text: Egypt's Masrawy carried the French interior ministry's count of 270,000 protesters outside Paris on 6 November, and franceinfo reported a fifth Saturday on 14 November, with marchers saying little was left once bills were paid. On 17 November Xinhua carried the ministry's figure of 146,000 at a new round, and Japan's Asahi Shimbun ran an essay from the Paris protests on why people go to demonstrations.

fragments.label: Spain, Portugal and Italy
fragments.text: El País reported on 11 November the unions' call to Spain's first general strike in 14 years, and Canada's CBC that millions struck over housing costs; on 12 November El País called the day unevenly followed. Observador reported Porto's housing camp putting up tents on 8 November and on 17 November asked whether the president had received the encampments to keep them quiet. Sky TG24 reported clashes and searches in 13 Italian cities on 14 November, and on 17 November MARCA quoted Irene Montero saying of price rises that 'something isn't working'.

fragments.label: Energy named, brackets frozen
fragments.text: Greece's iefimerida reported the European Commission's autumn forecast that an energy shock is eroding growth and raising inflation. Britain's Bournemouth Echo expected inflation to have risen on energy bills and a tobacco duty increase. Spain's El Mundo reported Brussels estimating that leaving income tax brackets unindexed will cost Spanish taxpayers more than 2.5 billion euros this year.

fragments.label: Top-ups rather than causes
fragments.text: Al Jazeera reported on 10 November that France brought forward a minimum wage rise in a bid to calm the protests. On 17 November Il Messaggero reported Meloni and Salvini at odds over Quota 64 and over paying 300 euros to the elderly with their pensions, Sky TG24 reported the last amendments to Italy's 2027 budget, and Handelsblatt reported a German reform to let benefits flow more easily. Each answer adds to incomes; none touches the energy price the Commission names or the rents behind the Iberian protests.

fragments.label: What two weeks show
fragments.text: No single day showed the shape: protest that began over French living costs moved to housing in Spain and Portugal and to policing in Italy, and in France fell from 270,000 counted outside Paris alone on 6 November to 146,000 in the 17 November round without stopping. A wave that shrinks after a concession but continues is one the concession has not settled. As El Mundo's report on Spain's brackets shows, the same prices also raise governments' tax take.

fragments.label: Different grievances
fragments.text: The countries do not share a cause. Spanish and Portuguese rents rose for a decade before the energy shock, through tourist lets and short supply; France's protests concern wages and prices; Italy's headlines are about police searches after clashes. Italy's pension payment and Germany's benefit reform were budget plans before any protest, and no headline calls them answers to the street.

fragments.label: Counts and coverage
fragments.text: Interior ministry counts are the government's own, and a smaller Tuesday figure may reflect the day of the week rather than a fading wave. Much of the coverage comes from foreign outlets reporting France, which can make a mainly French and Spanish story look like a European one.

horizons.label: Since 2020
horizons.text: The pandemic years ended in inflation: euro area prices rose 10.6% in the year to October 2022 after Russia's invasion pushed gas to record prices. Governments answered with shields rather than with action on supply: France capped regulated power and gas prices from late 2021, Spain and Portugal won the Iberian exception to cap gas in power prices in 2022, and Germany set aside 200 billion euros for energy relief. France's minimum wage rose by formula several times in 2022. By these headlines a second shock, from the war with Iran, arrived in 2026, and the Commission forecast reported by iefimerida says it is again cutting growth and raising inflation. What this decade put in place is the habit of answering an energy price with a transfer to households, which is why France's earlier minimum wage rise and Italy's 300 euros for pensioners were the first replies available.

horizons.label: Since 2008
horizons.text: The crisis of 2008 reached Spain and Portugal through housing. Spain's building boom ended in empty flats and evictions; Portugal took a bailout in 2011 under a troika programme that cut wages and pensions. In May 2011 the indignados camped in Madrid's Puerta del Sol; their movement fed Podemos, which entered government in 2020, and Irene Montero, quoted by MARCA this week, was one of its ministers. To earn foreign money both countries opened their housing to investors and tourists: Portugal's golden visas from 2012 and short lets in Lisbon and Porto, Spain's tourist flats in Barcelona and Málaga. Rents rose faster than wages through the 2010s. That is the ground under the Porto encampment and the 11 November general strike. Adam Tooze traces how the crisis became a decade of politics everywhere; in Iberia that politics settled on rent.

horizons.label: Since 1989
horizons.text: The Maastricht treaty of 1992 and the euro of 1999 took away the national currency as a tool. A country in the euro cannot devalue to cheapen its exports or let inflation shrink its debt, so adjustment comes through wages, taxes and transfers set in national budgets. That is why each government in these headlines answers on its own, through its own minimum wage, pension or tax brackets, even when the cause is shared. The same years ended automatic wage indexation in Italy, whose scala mobile was abolished in 1992, and left tax brackets in Spain to be indexed only when a government chose. The Commission's estimate in El Mundo, more than 2.5 billion euros from unindexed brackets this year, is that choice measured. The single currency made the price shock common to the four countries and left the response to each of them separately.

horizons.label: Since 1945
horizons.lens: WELFARE STATE / MINIMUM WAGE / THE STREET
horizons.text: Post-war western Europe built its welfare states on a bargain among unions, employers and governments: rising wages, pensions and public housing in return for industrial peace. France set a guaranteed minimum wage in 1950 and tied it to prices; after the strikes of May 1968 the Grenelle agreements raised it by about a third, the clearest case of the street winning a wage. Karl Polanyi argued in 1944 that societies pull markets back when prices threaten livelihoods, and Tony Judt's history shows how that idea became the post-war settlement. The gilets jaunes, who began on 17 November 2018, eight years before Xinhua's count of 146,000, won a cancelled fuel tax and 100 euros more for minimum-wage workers within a month and kept marching into 2019. The post-war order made a wage or pension rise the expected reply to protest; this fortnight tests whether that reply settles anything when the price comes from a war abroad.

built.subject: Weekly protests and strikes over living costs and housing in France, Germany, Spain, Portugal and Italy

readings.line: Outages from updates, flaws and attacks now come in the same week, and users cannot tell which kind has hit them.

watch.what: A company or agency revises its stated cause of an outage, from a fault to an attack or from an attack to a fault.
watch.because: If faults and attacks look alike at first, some first explanations given this month will turn out to be wrong.

watch.what: A government or regulator issues public guidance on checking whether an outage notice, alert or warning message is genuine.
watch.because: When users cannot tell a real failure or warning from a false one, the first official response should be advice on telling them apart.

ahead.precedent: On 19 July 2024 a faulty CrowdStrike update crashed about 8.5 million Windows computers, grounding flights and stopping hospitals; for hours many assumed a cyberattack until the company named the update. In December 2021 the Log4j flaw in a free Java library led governments to order emergency patching. The present differs because faults, flaws, attacks and hoaxes are arriving in the same days, during two wars and before a summit, so each failure is read as a possible attack.

paths.name: Each failure explained separately
paths.text: Over the next weeks Apple, the NSA and the attacked brands each give a separate technical account, no government links them, and the run leaves the news by December. Apple's same-day explanation and Trump's statement that everything is fine show the preference for separate, quick causes.
paths.sign: Apple or the NSA publishes a technical cause naming a single faulty change or component.

paths.name: An outage attributed to a state
paths.text: A failure first described as a fault is later attributed to Russia, Iran or China, as the war with Iran and the summit raise the stakes of attribution. It is less likely within weeks because attributions usually take months.
paths.sign: A government publicly attributes a service outage to a foreign state.

paths.name: Rapid disclosure made compulsory
paths.text: A government orders operators of major services to state the cause of outages within hours. Existing incident-reporting rules in the EU and US go to regulators, not the public, and nothing in the headlines suggests a change.
paths.sign: A government orders companies to publish the cause of major outages within a fixed number of hours.

ahead.decade: Over ten years, saying quickly and credibly whether a failure was a fault or an attack becomes a public service governments are expected to provide, as weather warnings are.

readings.change: Since 14 November the failures have widened from Microsoft and US air traffic to Apple, which blamed its own update, and to the NSA's classified network. A critical Java flaw has been treated as a security emergency in Seoul and Washington, and a cyberattack has hit 178 brands. The question has moved from who keeps the backup to whether anyone can tell a fault from an attack.
readings.claim: Apple suffered an outage it traced to a software update, the NSA's classified network went down on the eve of the Shenzhen summit, South Korea's National Security Office held an emergency meeting over a critical Java flaw while the US intelligence director said institutions were installing updates, and a cyberattack on HSBC, Zoom, CNN, IKEA and other brands tried to steal bank data. Onet reported 8,000 false bomb alarms at European schools and airports, and Trump said everything was fine. Faults, flaws, attacks and hoaxes are arriving together and look the same to the people they hit, so the first explanation given is often the only one the public hears.

events.label: Apple outage after software update
NSA classified network goes down
Critical Java flaw prompts emergency patching
Cyberattack on 178 global brands
False bomb alarms and blocked alerts
Reassurance and contingency plans in Washington

fragments.label: Apple and the NSA
fragments.text: The Sydney Morning Herald reported an Apple outage sparked by a software update, and Colombia's El Universal said it hit thousands of users worldwide. KPRC in Houston quoted a defence official saying the NSA's classified communications network went down, Hürriyet in Turkey reported its collapse, and UNIAN cited CNN calling it a serious intelligence failure on the eve of Trump's meeting with Xi and Putin.

fragments.label: A flaw and an attack
fragments.text: South Korea's Herald Economy reported the National Security Office holding an emergency government-civilian-military meeting over a critical Java vulnerability, and Lebanon's Al-Anbaa quoted the US Director of National Intelligence saying many institutions are installing updates. Argentina's LV12, Nigeria's Leadership, Spain's MARCA, Brazil's Diário do Grande ABC and Greece's iefimerida reported a cyberattack on HSBC, Zoom, CNN, IKEA and some 176 other brands, aimed at bank data, crypto and iPhones.

fragments.label: Warnings that mislead
fragments.text: Poland's Onet reported 8,000 false bomb alarms sent to schools and airports in Europe. Finland's Svenska Yle told readers their phone may have blocked a test alert but should not do so in a real situation. False warnings arrive by the thousand while a real one may not arrive at all.

fragments.label: Officials describe the risk differently
fragments.text: RNZ reported Trump saying everything is 'fine' as a string of tech outages raised alarms. Fortune reported that Kevin Warsh has Federal Reserve staff building contingencies for AI outcomes including bad actors attacking critical infrastructure. Two parts of the same government describe the same risk in opposite terms on the same day.

fragments.label: Same symptom, different cause
fragments.text: To a user a faulty update, an unpatched flaw and an attack look the same at first: a service stops or behaves strangely. Apple gave a cause the same day, the NSA outage was reported with none, and the brand campaign was named an attack because data was taken. The Java flaw is the case where a fault becomes an attack once someone uses it, which is why Seoul treated it as a security matter. With hoax alarms in the thousands, the public's first account of any failure is a guess.

fragments.label: Four different things
fragments.text: The events part on cause and intent: a self-inflicted update error with a stated cause, a criminal campaign with an obvious motive, a known flaw being patched, and an unexplained failure inside a secret agency. Apple named its cause within the day, which runs against the claim that users cannot tell. Outages happen every week; a week with a three-leader summit and a recent Microsoft failure simply gets more of them reported and read as connected.

horizons.label: Since 2020
horizons.text: In December 2020 investigators found that hackers had placed code in an update to SolarWinds network software used by thousands of organisations, including US government departments; the update channel itself was the attack. In May 2021 ransomware stopped the Colonial Pipeline. In December 2021 a flaw in Log4j, a free Java logging library inside millions of systems, led the US cybersecurity agency to order emergency patching across government. On 19 July 2024 a faulty CrowdStrike update crashed about 8.5 million Windows computers and grounded flights, and for hours many assumed an attack. By these headlines a Microsoft outage on 12 November and an American air traffic stoppage on 13 November preceded this week's failures. The decade taught that an update can be an attack and an attack can look like a bad update, which is why Seoul convened its military over a Java flaw and why the NSA outage, reported without a cause, was read as an intelligence failure.

horizons.label: Since 2008
horizons.text: The iPhone of 2007 and the App Store of 2008 put self-updating software on billions of devices, so one company's change reaches its users overnight, as Apple's did this week. The move of companies and banks onto a few cloud providers after 2008 concentrated the systems that fail together. The same years produced the model of an attack built to look like a fault: Stuxnet, found in 2010, made centrifuges at Natanz break in ways Iranian engineers first took for malfunction. Edward Snowden's disclosures in 2013 showed how much of the NSA's own work ran on contractors and shared systems. Shoshana Zuboff's account of the platforms helps explain why this week's campaign against 178 brands sought bank data and iPhones: the platforms gathered both in a few places. The period made failures larger because systems were shared, and harder to read because attacks learned to look like faults.

horizons.label: Since 1989
horizons.text: The web opened to the public in 1991, and in 1995 Sun Microsystems released Java on the promise that a program written once would run anywhere. That promise is why one Java flaw sits inside banks, phones and government systems at once, and why South Korea's National Security Office and the US intelligence director dealt with it on the same day. Netscape's share sale in August 1995 began the habit of building first and securing later, and the dot-com crash of 2000 left the software in place after many of the firms that wrote it had gone. The millennium bug of 1999 was the period's one large shared repair, done in advance and remembered as a scare because it worked. Ulrich Beck's account of societies that produce risks they cannot insure fits the shared code these years left behind: it is used by nearly every organisation and maintained by very few.

horizons.label: Since 1945
horizons.lens: EARLY WARNING / FALSE ALARMS / CIVIL DEFENCE
horizons.text: The Cold War built the first systems whose purpose was to tell an attack from a fault. After Sputnik in 1957 the United States founded ARPA and built radar chains meant to warn of missiles within minutes. They produced known errors: in November 1979 a training tape at NORAD showed a Soviet attack, and on 26 September 1983 Stanislav Petrov judged a Soviet satellite warning of American launches to be false. In both cases the decision whether a signal was real rested on a few officers. Civil defence sirens and public alert systems followed, of the kind Svenska Yle says Finnish phones may now block. The 8,000 false bomb alarms reported by Onet repeat the old problem at the scale of email, and the cost of each false signal falls on the schools and airports that must treat it as real.
